samples.text:
The graph shows the percentage of people who are 65 years old or more in Japan, Italy, USA and Mexico from 1960 to 2020, and also the projection until 2040.

In 1960 Italy and USA had the highest percentage, 9.3% and 9.2%. Japan had 5.7% and Mexico had only 3.4%. Japan increased very fast after 1980. It was 17.4% in 2000 and 23.0% in 2010, so it was more than Italy. In 2040 it is expected to be 35.3%, which is the highest.

Italy also increased steadily from 9.3% to 23.3% in 2020 and it will reach 32.1% in 2040. USA increase more slow than Italy and Japan. It was 12.4% in 2000 and 16.6% in 2020, and it will be 21.6% in 2040.

Mexico was the lowest in all period. It stayed below 5% until 2000, but then it started to grew and it is predicted to reach 14.2% in 2040.

Overall, the percentage of old people is increasing in all the countries and Japan has the biggest increase.
samples.why: Overview present but basic and late · key features and projections covered · adequate but repetitive vocabulary · errors in comparative adverbs, verb forms and articles that do not reduce clarity.

samples.text:
The line graph compares the proportion of people aged 65 and above in Japan, Italy, the USA and Mexico between 1960 and 2020, together with projections for 2030 and 2040.

Overall, the elderly share of the population has risen, and is expected to continue rising, in all four countries. Japan has experienced the most dramatic growth, moving from third place to first, while Mexico has had the youngest population throughout.

In 1960, older people made up 9.3% of the population in Italy and 9.2% in the USA, compared with 5.7% in Japan and 3.4% in Mexico. Japan's figure then grew rapidly, overtaking the USA in the 1990s and Italy by 2010, when it reached 23.0%. It is projected to climb to 35.3% by 2040, around six times the 1960 level.

Italy also saw a steady increase, and its proportion is forecast to reach 32.1% in 2040. The USA, by contrast, grew more slowly, hovering at roughly 12-13% from 1990 to 2010 and expected to reach 21.6%. Mexico's elderly population stayed below 5% until 2000, but it is predicted to grow faster in the future and reach 14.2%.
samples.why: Clear overview including Japan's change of rank · key features and projections well organised · some less common vocabulary · accurate, varied sentences with a minor slip in parallel structure.

samples.text:
The graph presents the percentage of the population aged 65 and over in Japan, Italy, the USA and Mexico from 1960 to 2020, as well as projected figures up to 2040.

Overall, all four populations have been ageing and are projected to continue doing so. The most notable development is Japan's rapid transformation from a relatively young society into the oldest of the four, whereas Mexico has consistently had the smallest proportion of older people.

In 1960, Italy and the USA had similar shares of over-65s, at 9.3% and 9.2% respectively, while the figures for Japan and Mexico were considerably lower, at 5.7% and 3.4%. Italy's proportion increased steadily, reaching 20.3% in 2010. Japan's, however, accelerated sharply from the 1980s onwards, surpassing Italy's by 2010 at 23.0%. The USA experienced slower and more uneven growth, with virtually no change between 1990 and 2000.

According to the projections, which begin in 2020, Japan will retain its lead, with over-65s forecast to make up 35.3% of the population by 2040, followed closely by Italy at 32.1%. The American figure is expected to rise to 21.6%, whereas Mexico, despite a quickening pace of ageing, is projected to reach only 14.2%.
samples.why: Skilful selection including Japan's overtaking and the projection note · clear, well-placed overview · accurate figures used comparatively · wide, precise vocabulary · wide range of error-free structures.
